title: Philemon
hook: Paul sends a runaway slave back as a beloved brother; Christians later drew on this against slavery, too slowly

segments.voice: Yesterday, neotes: be an example. Your line was be an example. Who did you tell what they do well? Day five hundred ninety-nine.

It's a single short chapter, written to one household, and it's about one man. His name was Onesimus. He was enslaved in the household of a Christian named Philemon. At some point he left, whether he ran away or went looking for Paul's help, the letter doesn't say. He ended up with Paul, who was in prison, and there he became a Christian. Now Paul is sending him back. And he sends him with this letter in his hand.
screen: `ONE SHORT CHAPTER, ONE MAN.` → `ONESIMUS LEAVES PHILEMON.` → `PAUL SENDS HIM BACK, WITH A LETTER.`

segments.voice: Paul could give orders, he says, but he'd rather ask. "I beseech thee for my son, whom I have begotten in my bands, Onesimus, Who hath been heretofore unprofitable to thee, but now is profitable both to me and thee." The name Onesimus means useful, so readers hear a pun: once useless to you, now useful. Then the heart of the letter: receive him "not now as a servant, but instead of a servant, a most dear brother." A brother, in the flesh and in the Lord. Then Paul puts his own name on the line: if he owes you anything, charge it to my account. I, Paul, write it with my own hand. I will repay it. Now the hard part, said plainly. Paul never commands Philemon to set Onesimus free. He says he's confident Philemon will do even more than he asks, and readers have argued ever since about whether that's a hint. We don't know what Philemon did. And this little letter was later used on both sides. Some slaveholders, including in the American South, cited it to defend returning people who had escaped. Others pointed to its words, no longer a servant but a brother, against slavery itself. Christians, the Catholic Church among them, came to condemn slavery too slowly. Popes condemned the slave trade in the nineteenth century, and the Second Vatican Council listed slavery among the things that poison human society and insult the Creator. Some years later, Ignatius of Antioch, writing to the church at Ephesus, named its bishop Onesimus. Some think it was the same man. Nobody can be sure.
screen: `ONESIMUS: 'USEFUL'.` · `NOT A SERVANT: A MOST DEAR BROTHER.` · `CHARGE IT TO MY ACCOUNT.` · `A LETTER USED ON BOTH SIDES.` · then, large: `NOT NOW AS A SERVANT, BUT A MOST DEAR BROTHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think about who you call brother. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the people you'd call brother or sister without thinking: family, close friends. Now widen the circle. Think of someone who serves you and whose name you don't know: a cleaner, a driver, a cashier, someone who picks the fruit you eat. Picture them as clearly as you can. Let the word brother or sister sit next to them. Notice what changes. If you pray, you can pray for them. If you don't, simply hold them in that word. The bell holds the time.
Philemon. Paul's short letter sending Onesimus back, not as a servant, but as a most dear brother. Today's word.
Your line: no longer a servant. Today, learn the name of one person who serves you, and use it. Day five hundred ninety-nine.

howItsDone: The Catholic Church today condemns slavery as an offense against human dignity (Gaudium et Spes 27; Catechism 2414), and remembers Philemon and Onesimus in its readings and saints' calendars.

original.note: Greek name meaning useful, profitable; Paul puns on it in Philemon 1:11.

trapdoor: what you thought: a short personal note nobody reads.
what it means: Paul asks a master to receive his slave as a beloved brother, and offers to pay his debts.
what a scholar hears: the Onesimus pun; no explicit call for manumission; used by both sides in the American slavery debates; Ignatius's bishop Onesimus.
